title: 14、18、24、32 TPI 怎麼選？鋸片齒數選擇的實務對照表
summary: 同一支鋸弓，換一片齒數不對的鋸片，壽命可能少一半。這篇用實際材料與管徑，說明 14 到 32 TPI 各自的適用範圍，以及什麼情況下該改用雙金屬。
body:
採購最常問的一個問題不是價格，而是「這支鋸片能切什麼」。答案幾乎都取決於兩個數字：齒數（TPI）與齒距。選錯齒數，不是切不動，就是切得慢、鋸片提早斷。

先看原則：同一個切口，至少要有 3 齒同時接觸

齒數太少的鋸片用在薄管上，齒尖會勾住管壁、把齒崩掉；齒數太多的鋸片切厚料，齒槽塞滿切屑、排不掉，鋸片就開始發熱、跑偏、斷裂。

實務上的判斷方式是看材料厚度，不是看材料種類：

材料厚度建議 TPI典型用途
< 3 mm（薄管、薄板、型材）24 – 32不鏽鋼薄管、銅管、電線管、角鐵
3 – 6 mm18 – 24一般鐵管、圓棒、螺栓
6 – 12 mm14 – 18厚壁管、實心圓鐵、軸件
> 12 mm14 或更低大料、鑄鐵、拆除工程

常見材料的實際建議

不鏽鋼管（薄壁）

用 24 或 32 TPI，並且低轉速、輕壓力。不鏽鋼會加工硬化，壓力一大、速度一快，切口表面立刻變硬，下一齒就切不動了。

一般鐵管、水電管

18 或 24 TPI 最順。18 TPI 排屑快、切得快；24 TPI 切口比較平整，適合之後要套牙或焊接。

實心圓鐵、螺栓

14 或 18 TPI。實心料最怕排屑不良，齒槽要够大。

PVC、塑膠管

24 TPI 以上，避免齒尖把管壁扯裂。切塑膠時用新鋸片反而容易黏屑，舊一點的鋸片更好用。

什麼時候一定要用雙金屬（Bi-Metal）

高碳鋼（HCS）鋸片硬度高、切口快、單價低，適合一般鐵、銅、塑膠與間歇使用。但遇到下面三種情況，我會建議直接換雙金屬：

  • 切不鏽鋼、工具鋼、軸承鋼：HCS 齒尖硬度够，但齒體韌性不足，容易崩齒。
  • 連續大量切割：例如工地一天切上百刀，HCS 會因為熱累積而快速鈍化。
  • 管子有震動、夾持不穩：雙金屬的齒體可以吸收衝擊，不會整片斷給你看。

反過來說，如果是一般維修、DIY、偶爾切幾刀，HCS 的性價比還是最高的——尤其是經過雙重熱處理（齒尖 HRC 63、齒體 HRC 38–42）的規格，韌性已經比傳統全硬化鋸片好很多。

三個現場常見的錯誤

  1. 用 32 TPI 切厚鐵：切得動，但慢到讓人放棄，而且齒槽塞屑後鋸片會過熱。
  2. 用 14 TPI 切薄不鏽鋼管：齒尖勾住管壁，一用力就崩齒，看起來像「鋸片品質不好」，其實是選錯。
  3. 新舊鋸片混用同一行程：舊鋸片已經磨鈍，會把新鋸片帶偏，切口越切越歪。

小結

記住一句話就好：薄料用密齒、厚料用疏齒；不鏽鋼放慢、實心料排屑。採購時如果不確定，把材料、厚度、一次要切幾刀告訴我們，我們可以直接建議對應的 TPI 與材質。
title_en: Choosing the Right TPI: 14, 18, 24 or 32 Explained
summary_en: The wrong tooth count can halve a blade's life. A practical table of which TPI to use for which material thickness, plus when high-carbon steel is not enough and bi-metal earns its price.
body_en:
The question we get most often from buyers is not about price — it is "what can this blade actually cut?" The answer usually comes down to two numbers: teeth per inch (TPI) and tooth pitch. Choose the wrong tooth count and the blade either will not cut, or cuts slowly and snaps early.

The rule: at least three teeth in the cut

A blade with too few teeth used on thin tube will catch the wall and strip its teeth. A blade with too many teeth used on thick stock fills its gullets with chips, cannot clear them, and starts to heat, wander and break.

In practice you judge by material thickness, not by material type:

ThicknessTPITypical work
Under 3 mm (thin tube, sheet, profile)24 – 32Thin stainless tube, copper pipe, conduit, angle iron
3 – 6 mm18 – 24General iron pipe, round bar, bolts
6 – 12 mm14 – 18Heavy-wall tube, solid bar, shafting
Over 12 mm14 or coarserHeavy stock, cast iron, demolition

By material

Thin-wall stainless tube

24 or 32 TPI, with low speed and light pressure. Stainless work-hardens: press hard or run fast and the cut surface hardens immediately, so the next tooth cannot bite.

General iron pipe and conduit

18 or 24 TPI works best. 18 TPI clears chips faster; 24 TPI leaves a flatter cut, which matters if you are threading or welding afterwards.

Solid bar and bolts

14 or 18 TPI. Solid stock suffers most from poor chip clearance, so the gullets need to be generous.

PVC and plastic pipe

24 TPI or finer so the teeth do not tear the wall. A slightly worn blade actually works better than a new one here, because a sharp tooth grabs and clogs.

When bi-metal is the only sensible choice

High-carbon steel (HCS) blades are hard, cut fast and cost less. They suit general iron, copper, plastics and intermittent use. In three situations, though, we recommend going straight to bi-metal:

  • Stainless, tool steel, bearing steel — the tooth tip is hard enough, but the body lacks toughness and chips.
  • Continuous high-volume cutting — hundreds of cuts a day on site heat-soaks an HCS blade and dulls it fast.
  • Vibration and poor clamping — a bi-metal body absorbs impact instead of snapping.

For maintenance, DIY and occasional cuts, HCS is still the best value — especially the dual heat-treated spec (teeth at HRC 63, body at HRC 38–42), which is far tougher than a fully hardened blade.

Three mistakes we see on site

  1. 32 TPI on thick steel — it cuts, but so slowly that people give up, and the clogged gullets overheat the blade.
  2. 14 TPI on thin stainless tube — the teeth catch the wall and strip. It looks like a quality problem; it is a selection problem.
  3. Mixing a worn blade with a new one — the dull blade drags the new one off line, and the cut drifts further with every stroke.

In one sentence

Fine teeth for thin stock, coarse teeth for thick stock; slow down for stainless, clear chips on solid bar. If you are unsure, tell us the material, the thickness and how many cuts per day, and we will recommend the TPI and blade type directly.
